# The final results {#sec-final}

**You will learn:**

- what was fixed before the development split was touched, and why it matters that nothing was changed afterwards;
- how the fine-tuned model compares with the untuned one on conversations that no choice of the book was made on;
- how much of the difference a good prompt makes up, and how much is left for fine-tuning;
- whether the validation numbers of the earlier chapters were optimistic;
- where the result sits among published numbers, and why that comparison is loose;
- which comparisons of the book are validation results only.

Every chapter so far reported the **validation** split, the one the book's choices were made on. This chapter is the
only one that uses the **development** split. Its conversations were set aside at the start (@sec-convfinqa), and its
gold programs were used only to test code that has no model in it. A model's outputs on them were not scored, and not read, until
the decisions below were written down.

## What was fixed first

Before any output was scored on the development split, the decisions of the book were written into the project's plan
(`PLAN.md`), with the commit they were made at, and a file was created whose existence is what lets the development evaluations run (the
builders refuse the split until it exists, and a test fails if any chapter before this one asks for it). From then on
the rule was that nothing changes because of a development number, except a bug, and a disappointing result is
reported and not fixed. The decisions were:

- **The model and its training.** The adapter of @sec-training: rank 16, trained for two epochs on the train-fit
  conversations, with the checkpoint of the lowest validation loss, and seed 0. The rank sweep of @sec-rank-sweep
  is a validation experiment and chose nothing.
- **The untuned model's prompt.** The variant that the rule of @sec-baseline-rule chose on validation, `e3p` (a
  plain system message and three examples, example set 0), and `e0p`, the prompt the fine-tuned model is trained with.
- **The output format.** The DSL of @sec-dsl, with greedy decoding, no grammar, and one attempt per turn; an invalid
  output counts as wrong (@sec-evaluating).
- **The measures.** Execution accuracy in both histories, with the predicted history as the headline; program
  accuracy next to it; a paired bootstrap that resamples whole report pages.

Six generation runs were then made, each once: the fine-tuned model, the untuned model with `e3p` and the untuned model
with `e0p`, each with the predicted history and with the gold history. The scores below are computed from them.

## The rule for more seeds

The fine-tuned model was trained once. Greedy decoding is deterministic, so the only noise that a second run would
add is the training's: the initialisation, the order of the data, the dropout. The book fixed in advance when that
noise would be measured: if the paired interval of the fine-tuned model against either untuned system includes
zero, in either history, two more training seeds are trained and scored on the same split, and the results are reported as a
mean and a spread. The rule is checked below, after the table.

## Results on the development split

```{python}
#HEAVY
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from convfinqa.artifacts import get
from convfinqa.data.splits import page_group
from convfinqa.stats import bootstrap_accuracy, paired_difference

RUNS_DEV = {
    ("untuned, e0p", "predicted"): "scores_untuned_dev_e0p_0_pred",
    ("untuned, e0p", "gold"): "scores_untuned_dev_e0p_0_gold",
    ("untuned, e3p", "predicted"): "scores_untuned_dev_e3p_0_pred",
    ("untuned, e3p", "gold"): "scores_untuned_dev_e3p_0_gold",
    ("fine-tuned", "predicted"): "scores_tuned_dev_main_0_pred",
    ("fine-tuned", "gold"): "scores_tuned_dev_main_0_gold",
}
SCORES = {
    ("untuned, e0p", "predicted"): get("scores_untuned_dev_e0p_0_pred"),
    ("untuned, e0p", "gold"): get("scores_untuned_dev_e0p_0_gold"),
    ("untuned, e3p", "predicted"): get("scores_untuned_dev_e3p_0_pred"),
    ("untuned, e3p", "gold"): get("scores_untuned_dev_e3p_0_gold"),
    ("fine-tuned", "predicted"): get("scores_tuned_dev_main_0_pred"),
    ("fine-tuned", "gold"): get("scores_tuned_dev_main_0_gold"),
}
dev = {k: list(h.jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for k, h in SCORES.items()}
dev_summary = {k: h.json("summary.json") for k, h in SCORES.items()}
program = {
    k: [{**s, "correct": s["program_correct"]} for s in v]
    for k, v in dev.items()
}
ci = {k: bootstrap_accuracy(v) for k, v in dev.items()}
ci_program = {k: bootstrap_accuracy(v) for k, v in program.items()}

n_turns = {len(v) for v in dev.values()}
dev_ids = {s["id"] for s in dev[("fine-tuned", "predicted")]}
n_conversations = len(dev_ids)
n_pages = len({page_group(i) for i in dev_ids})
# all six runs cover the same turns, every turn of the split
assert len(n_turns) == 1

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "history": [h for _, h in dev],
        "execution accuracy": [
            f"{ci[k]['accuracy']:.1%}" for k in dev
        ],
        "95% interval": [
            f"[{ci[k]['low']:.1%}, {ci[k]['high']:.1%}]" for k in dev
        ],
        "program accuracy": [
            f"{ci_program[k]['accuracy']:.1%}" for k in dev
        ],
        "invalid outputs": [
            f"{dev_summary[k]['invalid_rate']:.1%}" for k in dev
        ],
    },
    index=pd.Index([s for s, _ in dev], name="system"),
)
```

The split holds `{python} n_conversations` conversations, written from `{python} n_pages` report pages, and
`{python} n_turns.pop()` turns. In each row the interval
comes from resampling whole report pages 10,000 times (@sec-evaluating); it covers the choice of
pages, and not the training seed, which is the matter of the rule above.

```{python}
#HEAVY
contrasts = {}
for history in ("predicted", "gold"):
    for other in ("untuned, e3p", "untuned, e0p"):
        contrasts[(other, history)] = paired_difference(
            dev[("fine-tuned", history)], dev[(other, history)]
        )

# the fine-tuned model is ahead of both untuned systems, in both
# histories, by more than the resampling noise: the seed rule does not fire
assert all(c["low"] > 0 for c in contrasts.values())
# and the gold history is ahead of the predicted one
gap_hist = paired_difference(
    dev[("fine-tuned", "gold")], dev[("fine-tuned", "predicted")]
)
assert gap_hist["low"] > 0

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "difference": [
            f"{100 * c['difference']:+.1f}" for c in contrasts.values()
        ],
        "95% interval": [
            f"[{100 * c['low']:+.1f}, {100 * c['high']:+.1f}]"
            for c in contrasts.values()
        ],
    },
    index=pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
        [(f"fine-tuned minus {o}", h) for (o, h) in contrasts],
        names=["comparison", "history"],
    ),
).rename_axis(columns="points of execution accuracy")
```

With the predicted history, the headline mode, the fine-tuned model answers
`{python} f"{ci[('fine-tuned', 'predicted')]['accuracy']:.1%}"` of the turns correctly. The untuned model with the
best prompt answers `{python} f"{ci[('untuned, e3p', 'predicted')]['accuracy']:.1%}"`, and with the prompt the
fine-tuned model is trained with `{python} f"{ci[('untuned, e0p', 'predicted')]['accuracy']:.1%}"`. The paired
interval of the fine-tuned model against the first is
[`{python} f"{100 * contrasts[('untuned, e3p', 'predicted')]['low']:+.1f}"`,
`{python} f"{100 * contrasts[('untuned, e3p', 'predicted')]['high']:+.1f}"`] points, and against the second
[`{python} f"{100 * contrasts[('untuned, e0p', 'predicted')]['low']:+.1f}"`,
`{python} f"{100 * contrasts[('untuned, e0p', 'predicted')]['high']:+.1f}"`]. The other two intervals, with the gold
history, are in the table. **All four are far from zero, so the rule for more seeds did not fire, and the
fine-tuned model of the book is the one seed.** The gold history lifts the fine-tuned model to
`{python} f"{ci[('fine-tuned', 'gold')]['accuracy']:.1%}"`, `{python} f"{100 * gap_hist['difference']:+.1f}"` points
over its predicted-history score (paired interval [`{python} f"{100 * gap_hist['low']:+.1f}"`,
`{python} f"{100 * gap_hist['high']:+.1f}"`]): what the model loses to its own earlier mistakes, as on validation.

Program accuracy is lower than execution accuracy for every system, since it asks for the gold program and not only for
its answer (@sec-evaluating). The failures are of different kinds before and after fine-tuning:

```{python}
#HEAVY
from convfinqa.final_results import outcome_counts

outcomes = pd.DataFrame({
    f"{s}, {h}": outcome_counts(dev_summary[(s, h)])
    for (s, h) in dev
})
outcomes_pred = {s: outcome_counts(dev_summary[(s, "predicted")]) for s, _ in dev}
tuned = outcomes_pred["fine-tuned"]
wrong_tuned = sum(tuned.values()) - tuned["correct"]

# the untuned model loses most turns to the format of its answer; what is
# left after fine-tuning is mostly valid programs that are wrong
assert outcomes_pred["untuned, e0p"]["invalid output"] \
    > outcomes_pred["untuned, e0p"]["correct"]
assert tuned["invalid output"] <= 0.05 * wrong_tuned
assert tuned["wrong numbers"] == max(
    tuned[k] for k in (
        "wrong operations", "wrong numbers", "wrong answer, right shape"
    )
)
outcomes
```

With the prompt it is trained on, the untuned model writes a program that runs in
`{python} sum(outcomes_pred["untuned, e0p"][k] for k in ("correct", "wrong operations", "wrong numbers", "wrong answer, right shape"))`
of its `{python} sum(outcomes_pred["untuned, e0p"].values())` turns, so most of its mistakes are the format of the
answer. After fine-tuning, `{python} tuned["invalid output"]` of the `{python} wrong_tuned` wrong turns are not a
program, and the largest group is valid programs with other numbers (`{python} tuned["wrong numbers"]`). As on
validation, what fine-tuning leaves behind is a reading and reasoning failure, not a writing failure. The book does not
label these dev errors one by one: the error analysis of @sec-evaluating-errors was done on validation, so that no
development failure was read before the freeze.

## How much of the gap does a prompt close?

The untuned model with `e0p` and the fine-tuned model see the same input, so the distance between them is what
fine-tuning adds. The untuned model with `e3p` has the best prompt that validation found. How much of that distance has
the prompt already covered?

```{python}
#HEAVY
from convfinqa.final_results import share_of_gap_closed

closed = {
    h: share_of_gap_closed(
        dev[("untuned, e0p", h)], dev[("untuned, e3p", h)], dev[("fine-tuned", h)]
    )
    for h in ("predicted", "gold")
}
# the prompt closes a large part of the distance, but not all of it:
# the interval stays between 1/2 and 1 in both histories
assert all(0.5 < c["low"] and c["high"] < 1 for c in closed.values())

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "gap, fine-tuned minus e0p": [
            f"{100 * c['gap']:.1f} points" for c in closed.values()
        ],
        "covered by the e3p prompt": [
            f"{c['share']:.0%}" for c in closed.values()
        ],
        "95% interval": [
            f"[{c['low']:.0%}, {c['high']:.0%}]" for c in closed.values()
        ],
    },
    index=pd.Index(list(closed), name="history"),
)
```

With the predicted history the prompt covers `{python} f"{closed['predicted']['share']:.0%}"` of the distance, and with
the gold history `{python} f"{closed['gold']['share']:.0%}"`. Most of what fine-tuning adds can be had from a good prompt
with three examples, and the rest, the part that the prompt cannot reach, is
`{python} f"{100 * (contrasts[('untuned, e3p', 'predicted')]['difference']):.1f}"` points with the predicted history. Two
things limit how far to read this. The prompt was developed on validation over several variants, while the
fine-tuning configuration was fixed in advance, which favours the prompt. And the prompt is limited to describing the
language: it does not teach the annotation conventions that the fine-tuning data show (@sec-baseline), which a longer prompt
could. The two routes also cost different amounts at inference: the examples make the prompt longer than the fine-tuned
model's (@sec-evaluating measures it on validation).

## Next to published results

The published numbers come from different set-ups, so this is a loose comparison. FinQANet [@chen2022convfinqa] is
given facts retrieved from the page, and its gold-facts variant and the few-shot GPT-3 of the same paper are given the
facts that the annotators marked; ours reads the whole page. Our predicted history is the closest to how a
published system would be used, and the gold history is an upper bound. Fin-R1 uses its own protocol (below). Nothing here is a leaderboard.

```{python}
#| label: fig-published
#| fig-cap: "Execution accuracy on ConvFinQA, published results (grey diamonds, with what each paper says about its evaluation set) and three systems of this book on the development split (circles and a square, with the 95% interval). The set-ups differ: the published results are not run on the same input."
#| fig-alt: "Dot chart of execution accuracy, one row per system, sorted from lowest to highest. Published results are grey diamonds, this book's systems are coloured with horizontal intervals. The fine-tuned model with predicted history sits between the published systems."
#HEAVY
from convfinqa.final_results import PUBLISHED

ours = [
    (
        "this book, fine-tuned, predicted history",
        ("fine-tuned", "predicted"), "#b85450", "o"
    ),
    (
        "this book, fine-tuned, gold history (upper bound)",
        ("fine-tuned", "gold"), "#3b6ea5", "o"
    ),
    (
        "this book, untuned, e3p, predicted history",
        ("untuned, e3p", "predicted"), "#b85450", "s"
    ),
]
rows = [
    (f"{p['label']} ({p['split']})", p["accuracy"], None, None, "#6b6b6b", "D")
    for p in PUBLISHED
] + [
    (
        label, 100 * ci[k]["accuracy"], 100 * ci[k]["low"],
        100 * ci[k]["high"], colour, marker
    )
    for label, k, colour, marker in ours
]
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r[1])
ours_rank = {
    name: i for i, (name, *_) in enumerate(rows) if name.startswith("this book")
}
fine_tuned_rank = ours_rank["this book, fine-tuned, predicted history"]
published_above = sum(
    1 for name, value, *_ in rows
    if not name.startswith("this book") and value > rows[fine_tuned_rank][1]
)
published_below = sum(
    1 for name, value, *_ in rows
    if not name.startswith("this book") and value < rows[fine_tuned_rank][1]
)

# the fine-tuned model sits inside the published range, not at an end of it
assert published_above > 0 and published_below > 0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.6))
for i, (name, value, low, high, colour, marker) in enumerate(rows):
    if low is not None:
        ax.hlines(i, low, high, color=colour, linewidth=2, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(
        value, i, marker, color=colour, markersize=7, zorder=3,
        markerfacecolor=(
            "white" if name.startswith("this book, untuned")
            else colour
        ),
    )
    ax.text(
        value + (2.5 if low is None else (high - value) + 1.5), i, f"{value:.1f}",
        va="center", fontsize=8, color="#444444"
    )
ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)), [r[0] for r in rows], fontsize=8)
for tick, (name, *_) in zip(ax.get_yticklabels(), rows):
    if name.startswith("this book"):
        tick.set_fontweight("bold")
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("execution accuracy (%)")
ax.grid(axis="x", color="#dddddd", linewidth=0.6)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for side in ("top", "right", "left"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

On development, with the predicted history, the fine-tuned model is ahead of `{python} published_below` of the
`{python} len(PUBLISHED)` published rows and behind `{python} published_above`; the gold-history point is an upper
bound and is not comparable with them. The bold rows are ours. Two things keep the comparison loose: the inputs
differ (above), and some rows do not say which split they use (FinQANet) or use a sample of 200 questions (the two human
rows). @fig-published is a map of where the number sits and not a ranking: a difference of a couple of points between
rows is not a finding.

The ConvFinQA paper [@chen2022convfinqa] gives the crowd, GPT-3, FinQANet and human rows (GPT-3 from its Table 5, the
others from its Table 3), @li2023gpt the GPT-4 row, and @khatuya2025finder the PoT-GPT-4, ENCORE and FINDER rows.
Fin-R1 [@liu2025finr1] also reports a ConvFinQA figure, but its answers are judged by a language model on a random
sample whose split it does not state, so it measures something else and is left out.

## Were the validation numbers optimistic?

The choices of the book were made on validation: the prompt, the checkpoint, the grammar, the format. If a choice had
fitted the validation conversations in a way that does not carry over, the development numbers would be lower. The
check is the same three systems, both histories, on the two splits. The splits hold different pages, so each
accuracy is resampled on its own, and the interval is for the difference of the two.

```{python}
#HEAVY
from convfinqa.final_results import split_difference

VAL_SCORES = {
    ("untuned, e0p", "predicted"): get("scores_untuned_val_e0p_0_pred"),
    ("untuned, e0p", "gold"): get("scores_untuned_val_e0p_0_gold"),
    ("untuned, e3p", "predicted"): get("scores_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred"),
    ("untuned, e3p", "gold"): get("scores_untuned_val_e3p_0_gold"),
    ("fine-tuned", "predicted"): get("scores_tuned_val_main_0_pred"),
    ("fine-tuned", "gold"): get("scores_tuned_val_main_0_gold"),
}
val = {k: list(h.jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for k, h in VAL_SCORES.items()}
ci_val = {k: bootstrap_accuracy(v) for k, v in val.items()}
moved = {k: split_difference(dev[k], val[k]) for k in dev}
significant = [k for k, m in moved.items() if m["excludes_zero"]]
# the sentence below names the exception: the untuned model with the training prompt, which does not move with the training
assert significant

# nothing that validation chose is significantly worse on dev: the two
# systems that went through the book's choices (the fine-tuned model and the
# prompt picked on validation) stay within the noise
assert not any(s in ("fine-tuned", "untuned, e3p") for s, _ in significant)
# and the fine-tuned model scores lower on dev than on val in both histories,
# as selection on val would make it, though not by more than the noise
assert all(
    moved[("fine-tuned", h)]["difference"] < 0 for h in ("predicted", "gold")
)

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "validation": [f"{ci_val[k]['accuracy']:.1%}" for k in dev],
        "development": [f"{ci[k]['accuracy']:.1%}" for k in dev],
        "difference": [f"{100 * moved[k]['difference']:+.1f}" for k in dev],
        "95% interval": [
            f"[{100 * moved[k]['low']:+.1f}, {100 * moved[k]['high']:+.1f}]"
            for k in dev
        ],
    },
    index=pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(list(dev), names=["system", "history"]),
).rename_axis(columns="execution accuracy, points for the last two")
```

The fine-tuned model is `{python} f"{-100 * moved[('fine-tuned', 'predicted')]['difference']:.1f}"` points lower on
development than on validation with the predicted history and
`{python} f"{-100 * moved[('fine-tuned', 'gold')]['difference']:.1f}"` with the gold history, and the untuned model with
`e3p` differs by `{python} f"{100 * moved[('untuned, e3p', 'predicted')]['difference']:+.1f}"` and
`{python} f"{100 * moved[('untuned, e3p', 'gold')]['difference']:+.1f}"`. None of these four intervals excludes zero, so the
data cannot tell a small optimism of selection from the difference between two samples of pages; they show that
the validation numbers were not far off. `{python} len(significant)` of the six differences has an interval that does
exclude zero: `{python} ", ".join(f"{s} with the {h} history" for s, h in significant) or "none"`. That is the
untuned model with the prompt of the fine-tuned model, which no choice of the book depended on, and it is the floor of
the comparison, so a few points of difference does not change what the chapter concludes.

## What this chapter does not report

Only the comparison above is run on the development split. The other comparisons of the book are results on validation,
reported where they are made, and the book does not claim them for the development split: the untuned prompt
variants, the `e3p` prompt on the fine-tuned model and the extra-compute rows (@sec-evaluating); the DSL against Python,
untuned and fine-tuned (@sec-python-format); the grammar rows (@sec-constrained-decoding); the merged adapter; and the
rank sweep (@sec-rank-sweep). The reason is the same for all: a result on the development split is a result that is
reported, once, and the more comparisons are run on it, the more of its value as a check is spent.

The result is also limited in three ways. It is one training seed, so the interval of a number is for the choice of
pages and does not include the noise of training; the rule for more seeds did not call for them, but a
second seed is what would measure it. The prompt of the untuned model
had one example set. And the numbers are on one benchmark, with one model, so the contrast with published work
is of a set-up and not of a method.
